html:
In early 1258 a Mongol army under Hulegu besieged and sacked Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. The city fell within a few weeks and was plundered for about a week.

Hulegu had been sent west by his brother, the Great Khan, to bring the Muslim lands to heel. The caliph al-Mustasim refused to submit and had little army to back his refusal. The Mongols brought skilled siege engineers, broke the walls and took the city in February. The caliph was killed, by tradition rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses so that no royal blood was spilled. The number of other dead is unknown; sources speak of hundreds of thousands, which is surely an exaggeration, but the killing was enormous.

Libraries were destroyed, among them the House of Wisdom. A later story says the Tigris ran black with ink. Baghdad, founded in 762 and once among the largest cities on earth, never regained its old place.

The fall is often called the end of the Islamic golden age. Historians now see it as less sharp a break: Cairo, Tabriz and other cities carried learning on, and Hulegu's own Ilkhanate became a patron of science. Two years later the Mamluks stopped the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut, and a line of Abbasid caliphs was revived in Cairo under their protection.
sum: In early 1258 a Mongol army under Hulegu besieged and sacked Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. The city fell within a few weeks and was plundered for about a week.
